list.listitem: Causes of antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH) range from transient physiologic changes to severe underlying pathology; therefore, a thorough evaluation is warranted. C
Perform postnatal ultrasounds during the first week and first month of life in infants previously diagnosed with ANH. If both tests come back normal, no further workup is necessary. C
In patients with persistent hydronephrosis with normal voiding cystourethrogram and renography, serial ultrasounds may be performed to monitor resolution or persistence of hydronephrosis. C

Prophylactic antibiotics can be considered for children with high-grade hydronephrosis to prevent urinary tract infection (UTI). B Prophylactic antibiotics have not been shown to improve outcomes in persistent postnatal hydronephrosis (PNH) due to vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). B
Surgical approaches to persistent hydronephrosis from ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction or posterior urethral valves include pyeloplasty and endoscopic valve ablation. C

Hydronephrosis is an abnormal dilatation of the renal pelvis and/or calyces, at times accompanied by changes in the renal parenchyma. Strictly, the term is a radiologic finding and does not necessarily imply pathology. Clinically significant antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH) has been proposed as being >10 mm in the second trimester and >15 mm in the third trimester; these values are associated with a >50% likelihood of ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction on postnatal imaging.
Antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH) is detected in 0.5% to 1.0% of routine prenatal ultrasounds. This is higher in infants with other major fetal anomalies.

Among those found to have ANH, the prevalence of vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is 16.2%; a similar percentage of reflux (17%) is seen even with a normal postnatal ultrasound. However, in mild ANH (SFU grade 1 or 2), the incidence of VUR is only 3%.
In patients who have VUR, the prevalence of VUR in siblings is 27.4% and in offspring is 35.7%.
Antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH) is often a transient (48%) or physiologic (15%) condition.
Pathology is suggested by the presence of oligohydramnios or additional renal or extrarenal anomalies.

Common causes for postnatal persistence of hydronephrosis include ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction (10-45%), VUR (9-30%), megaureter (4-10%), multicystic dysplastic kidney (2%), ureterocele, and posterior urethral valves (1-2%). (see ).
Several syndromes, most rare, are associated with hydronephrosis including Turner syndrome, Urofacial syndrome, and Au-Kline syndrome (hypotonia, abnormal facial features, autonomic dysfunction).

In one prospective study, renal anomalies were detected in 136 out of 587 cases identified with major fetal anomalies antenatally. ANH was the most commonly seen anomaly (44.8%) followed by bilateral cystic kidney (36.7%).
Hydronephrosis results from anatomic or functional interruption of urine flow anywhere in the urinary tract, from the kidneys to the urethral meatus.

Persistent pressure transmitted to the renal tubules causes renal parenchymal changes such as ischemia and compression atrophy. These processes eventually lead to renal parenchymal scarring and compromised renal function.
Screening for antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH) is performed as part of a prenatal anatomy scan.
Follow up for abnormalities noted on ultrasound is discussed below in Approach to the Patient.
Circumcision may reduce the risk of urinary tract infection (UTI) in boys with hydronephrosis.

Several studies have noted that circumcision status appears to be a protective factor against UTI in boys with hydronephrosis. However, many of these studies were designed to evaluate continuous antibiotic prophylais rather than circumcision and had insufficient data to assess the effects of circumcision status.
In one cohort study of children with primary VUR, UTI occurred in 6/27 (22%) of boys after circumcision compared to 17/25 (68%) without circumcision.

The most comprehensive study to date is a retrospective insurance claims study of 5561 newborn boys with hydronephrosis matched to 11,120 healthy controls. Approximately 42.9% of the boys with hydronephrosis had undergone newborn circumcision. Among those with hydronephrosis, NNT to prevent 1 UTI was 10, compared with a NNT of 83 for healthy boys without hydronephrosis. This association was consistent across various hydronephrosis diagnoses including isolated hydronephrosis (OR = 0.35, NNT = 13), VUR (OR = 0.35, NNT = 6), and UPJ obstruction (OR = 0.35, NNT = 9).
See Drug Therapy for information on antibiotic prophylaxis.
In patients diagnosed with antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH), perform postnatal ultrasounds in the first week and first month of life. If both tests come back normal, no further workup is necessary. C
Obtain voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) in infants with postnatal hydronephrosis (PNH) beyond the first month of life. C

Diuretic renography may be performed to further characterize renal function in patients with moderate to severe PNH without VUR. A differential renal function (DRF) less than 40% signifies compromised renal function. C
In patients with persistent hydronephrosis with normal VCUG and renography, serial ultrasounds may be performed to monitor resolution or persistence of hydronephrosis. C
The two most common grading systems to assess severity of antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH) are the Society of Fetal Urology (SFU) and the anteroposterior pelvic diameter (APPD) grading systems. (see ).

A newer Urinary Tract Dilation (UTD) classification system has been validated as a single grading system that can be used across the antenatal and postnatal time periods to describe urinary tract dilation(See ). It may have improved inter-rater reliability compared with the SFU grading system.

Another grading system, Onen, has been suggested to overcome the difficulties with interrater variability associated with SFU and inaccuracies of AP diameter measurement that can vary based on hydration, bladder filling, position, and respiration. This grading system describes two categories of kidney findings – dilation of the pelvicalyceal system (pelvic alone or pelvis and caliceal) and renal parenchyma thickness (medullary and/or cortical thinning) and appearance (echogenicity, cortical cysts, corticomedullary differentiation which are suggestive of renal damage). These parameters are classified into 4 grades, with follow-up and treatment based on grade. Validation is needed.
The initial screening for ANH is part of second trimester prenatal anatomic ultrasound.

ANH is followed postnatally by renal and bladder ultrasound (RBUS) in the first week of life and at 1 month of life. With the exception of severe antenatal findings such as high-grade hydronephrosis, additional anomalies, or bilateral hydronephrosis, the first postnatal ultrasound should be deferred until 48 hours of life to avoid underestimating the degree of hydronephrosis due to physiologic oliguria present shortly after birth.
For those with mild postnatal hydronephrosis (SFU 1-2), ultrasound surveillance alone is recommended.

Repeat ultrasound at 1 month of life is recommended to detect late progression of hydronephrosis. Risk of progression is 1-5%, and when late worsening of hydronephrosis occurs, it is often clinically significant.

The UTD classification system, updated in 2021, uses six ultrasound findings to describe urinary tracts (Table 3). Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 articles including 2165 children found that high-risk UTD was associated with both surgical intervention (OR 21.4, 95% CI 15.7-29.2) and UTIs (OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.6-2.8). Combined intermediate and high-risk UTD were also associated with both outcomes
In patients with postnatal hydronephrosis beyond the first month of life, VCUG may be performed to check for VUR.
Sonographic findings of hydroureter, duplication, renal dysmorphia, and uroepithelial thickening of the renal pelvis can be used to predict high-grade VUR.
The need for a VCUG in cases of UPJ obstruction is controversial due to the low incidence of concomitant VUR in these cases.
Presence of VUR on VCUG may be further evaluated using the technetium dimercaptosuccinic acid scan to investigate for renal scarring.

Diuretic renography, also referred to as diuretic renal scintigraphy (DRS), may be performed to further characterize renal function and presence of obstruction in patients without VUR but with moderate to severe PNH.

DRS provides a way to estimate renal function. Differential renal function (DRF) obtained from renography studies measures the relative tracer uptake from the blood by the kidneys. A DRF less than 40% usually denotes compromised renal function. Delayed washout time of radiotracer (half-time >20 minutes) after diuretic administration on nuclear scans usually denotes obstruction.

It is generally recommended that children with mild hydronephrosis (SFU 1-2 or APPD = 5-9 mm) do not need any functional imaging studies such as DRS. However, Society for Fetal Urology guidelines state that with moderate hydronephrosis (SFU 3 or APPD ≥10 mm), DRS may be useful to stratify risk of surgery. Most clinicians agree that severe hydronephrosis (SFU 4) should be evaluated with functional studies.
DRS is typically deferred until at least 6 weeks of life to allow for maturation of the kidneys and to maximize accuracy of the study.

In patients without VUR but with persistent mild hydronephrosis (APPD = 5-9 mm) and in patients with moderate to severe PNH (APPD ≥10 mm) but with normal DRS, serial ultrasounds may be performed to monitor resolution or persistence of hydronephrosis.

Efforts are underway to better refine ultrasound prediction of outcomes with hybrid metrics. Examples include combining APPD and caliectasis to predict infants who are at higher risk of progressing to surgery and following the renal parenchyma-to-hydronephrosis ratio over time to monitor stability.

Magnetic resonance urography demonstrated 95% sensitivity and 100% specificity in detecting the presence, level, and grade of hydronephrosis; the test, performed without contrast, also showed good agreement (κ = 0.66) with intravenous urography.
Shear-wave elastography of the kidneys is not useful for discriminating obstructive from non-obstructive hydronephrosis in one study of 37 children, using DRS as the reference standard.

Urine proteomic tests are under investigation as tools to enhance prediction of VUR or UPJ obstruction in infants with hydronephrosis, as well as for surveillance and detection of worsening renal injury.

Potential markers for identifying UPJ obstruction include epidermal growth factor (EGF), monocyte chemotactic peptide-1 (MCP-1), urinary transforming growth factor-β1, urinary angiotensinogen, and serum CA 19-9.

Metabolic markers involved in mitochondrial energy metabolism (β-F1-ATPase and electron transfer flavoprotein β subunit) may also be useful markers of worsening renal injury in children with congenital hydronephrosis.
Biomarkers potentially useful in identifying VUR include levels of matrix metalloproteinase MMP9 and its inhibitor TIMP1, urinary levels of MMP9, MMP9/Cr, MMP9/TIMP1, and MMP9/TIMP1/Cr ratios.
See . A diagnostic evaluation should be conducted postnatally for infants diagnosed with ANH on prenatal ultrasound. See table for differential diagnosis.
Abnormal ultrasounds on the first week and first month of life are strongly predictive of a subsequent diagnosis of nephrouropathy.

In contrast, normal ultrasounds during the first week and first month provide moderate evidence against subsequent nephrouropathy. Furthermore, normal ultrasound at week 1 and 1 month provide moderate evidence against subsequent abnormality on VCUG.

Parental counseling is one of the most important aspects in the care of infants with hydronephrosis. It is important to explain to the parents the timing of the different tests, their accuracy, and their implications on management and prognosis.
Treatment of antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH) depends on the underlying cause; a thorough evaluation is critical. C
Prenatal counseling is one of the most important aspects in the management of ANH. C
Prophylactic antibiotics can be considered for children with high-grade hydronephrosis to prevent UTI, with a number needed to treat (NNT) of 7 to prevent one UTI. B
Prophylactic antibiotics have not been shown to improve outcomes in persistent postnatal hydronephrosis (PNH) due to VUR. B
Pyeloplasty appears to be successful in most children with UPJ obstruction, with complete resolution in about half. C

While continuous antibiotic prophylaxis (CAP) is recommended to prevent UTIs in infants with ANH and an elevated risk of UTI, these recommendations have been primarily based on low- to moderate-quality studies with high risk of bias.
Those at highest risk of developing UTI are uncircumcised boys, all girls, those with moderate-to-severe (SFU 3-4 or APPD ≥10 mm), familial VUR, and additional anatomic anomalies.

The best available evidence suggests selective use of antibiotics based on severity. Authors of a systematic review of 21 studies found that UTI rates were similar regardless of use of antibiotic prophylaxis for children with low-grade hydronephrosis (2.2% on prophylaxis vs. 2.8% without). However, for children with high-grade (SFU 3-4) hydronephrosis, those receiving prophylaxis had a significantly lower UTI rate than those those not receiving CAP (14.6%, 95% CI 9.3-22.0 vs. 28.9%, 95% CI 24.6-33.6) with a NNT to prevent one UTI of 7.

A nonblinded RCT with 100 patients showed that antibiotic prophylaxis in PNH does not decrease the likelihood of developing pyelonephritis or decrease the incidence of renal damage in children younger than 30 months in the setting of VUR.

In the Randomized Intervention for Children with Vesicoureteral Reflux (RIVUR) trial, investigators enrolled 607 children aged 2-71 months with grade 1-4 VUR diagnosed after a first or second febrile or symptomatic UTI and randomized them to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or placebo for 2 years. At study end, 58 (10%) of 599 children had renal scarring, but new renal scarring did not differ between groups (6% vs. 7%, respectively).

In a re-analysis of the RIVUR trial data, investigators found that recurrent UTI was associated new renal scarring which occurred in 5 of 244 (2%) patients on antibiotic prophylaxis and 13 of 245 (5%) on placebo. However, there were no differences between groups in scar severity at final scan or change from baseline. The difference in the report of new renal scarring between these analyses was the inclusion of only children with recurrent UTI in this analysis, as some children in the original RIVUR trial developed new scarring without recurrent UTI.

In an RCT of 49 infants who had undergone primary endoscopic valve ablation for posterior urethral valves, those randomized to oxybutynin vs. placebo had a greater likelihood of hydronephrosis improvement (61.9% vs 34.8%) and vesicoureteral reflux resolution (62.5% vs 25%), but there was no significant difference in febrile UTI (29.2% vs 40%). The drug was discontinued in 5 children due to facial flushing in 2, bladder and upper tract dilatation in 2, and cognitive changes in 1 child.

Patients with abnormal DRS (DRF<40% or T1/2>20min) can be considered for pyeloplasty (excision of the stenotic area of the renal pelvis or UPJ and reattaching the normal caliber ureter or creating a conduit using tissue from the remaining ureter and renal pelvis).

Authors of a literature review were unable to identify a best approach to pyeloplasty, noting advantages to surgeon well-being and ergonomics and ease of suturing with the robotic approach but quicker time frame and ability to use a small incision when performing open surgery in infants.

In a case series of 212 children with hydronephrosis meeting inclusion criteria at a single institution, 58 were performed with robotic-assisted laparoscopy and 154 with conventional open pyeloplasty. Complete resolution and success rates were 62% and 74% in the former group and 45% and 70% in the latter. In the matched cases, complete resolution occurred more often and improvement occurred more quickly in cases undergoing robotic-assisted laparoscopic pyeloplasty.

Infants with UPJ obstruction requiring surgery were found to have similar rates of successful resolution, complications, post-surgical catheter use, and reintervention in a meta-analysis comparing 440 infants who underwent minimally-invasive surgery (laparoscopic/robotic pyeloplasty) to 3054 infants who underwent open surgery.

For children with hydronephrosis from posterior urethral valves, primary endoscopic valve ablation or urinary drainage intervention is performed. In one retrospective case series of 685 children hospitalized at a median age of 7 (interquartile range, 1-37) days with congenital urethral stenosis who underwent endoscopic valve ablation or urinary drainage, 34 children (5%) died, most from associated pulmonary hypoplasia.
Intrauterine surgical intervention is rarely indicated and should only be performed in well-experienced centers.

Given the complexity of the diagnostic evaluation and the potential for permanent renal scarring, patients with persistent PNH should be referred to a specialist (eg, pediatric urologist or nephrologist).

Newborns with an APPD of <10 mm, especially in combination with SFU grade of 1-2, can be safely discharged from the newborn nursery as they are unlikely to experience complications based on a single center, retrospective study of 18 infants with hydronephrosis. In this study, none of the children meeting these parameters eventually required pyeloplasty.
Most infants with idiopathic ANH (SFU 1-2) will improve spontaneously; however, 20% to 25% will require surgical intervention (mostly SFU 3-4). C

In one case series of 1441 infants with ANH, 62% of renal units on the initial postnatal ultrasound had transient or non-obstructive hydronephrosis. Higher degrees of hydronephrosis correlated with increased risk of urological pathologies. C

In one study of 96 infants with 129 kidneys with isolated hydronephrosis, spontaneous resolution rates for kidneys with insignificant hydronephrosis were 24%, 40%, and 68% at ages 6, 12, and 24 months, respectively. Anteroposterior renal pelvic diameter was the only independent factor predicting resolution with a hazard ratio of 0.83 (95 % CI 0.74-0.92). C
In a cohort study of 822 children with congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, chronic kidney disease occurred in 6% at a median follow-up of 43 months. C

Moderate and severe ANH carries a significant risk of postnatal pathology; hence, comprehensive postnatal management should be undertaken. In one case series of 178 infants with ANH, virtually all 119 infants (97.5%) with mild ANH had postnatal ultrasound results showing normal or mild hydronephrosis. Of those with moderate ANH, 20% had moderate PNH and the rest showed improvement. Those with severe ANH (renal pelvic diameter >20 mm; 10 infants) had a high incidence (90%) of moderate and severe PNH. C
At one institution, 9% of boys with a postnatal diagnosis of posterior urethral valve who underwent urethral valve ablation developed chronic kidney disease. C

In the study of 685 children who underwent endoscopic valve ablation or urinary drainage for posterior urethral valves, 34 (5%) children died, most from associated pulmonary hypoplasia, 59 (9%) children underwent one or more dialysis catheter placements, and 36 (7%) children underwent kidney transplant at a median age of 3 (interquartile range, 2-8) years, most from associated kidney dysplasia. C

In a follow-up study of 192 children with ANH (135 with nonrefluxing hydronephrosis, 21 with nonrefluxing hydroureteronephrosis, and 36 with VUR), 24 (13%) developed at least one UTI at a mean follow-up of 2.6 (0.3-11.2) years. In another 1-year follow-up study of 213 patients with ANH, UTI developed in 8%, more frequently in females, uncircumcised males, and with the presence of parenchymal renal cyst. C

In another case series of 256 children detected antenatally with urinary tract abnormalities, about one third of the children with PNH had evidence of renal parenchymal defects. However, there was no difference in the development of acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, or need for surgery or dialysis treatment between infants with and without hydronephrosis. C

feature.caption: Systems for Grading the Severity of Antenatal Hydronephrosis.
feature.feature_body:
Society of Fetal Urology Grading System
Hydronephrosis Features
Grade 0 No hydronephrosis; intact central renal complex seen on ultrasonographic examination (USG)
Grade 1 Only renal pelvis visualized; dilated pelvis on USG; no caliectasis on intravenous pyelogram (IVP)
Grade 2 Moderately dilated renal pelvis and a few calices seen on IVP
Grade 3 Hydronephrosis with nearly all calyces seen; large renal pelvis and good parenchyma on USG; large calyces seen on IVP
Grade 4 Hydronephrosis with nearly all calyces seen; with accompanying parenchymal atrophy or thinning
Anteroposterior Pelvic Diameter Grading System
Hydronephrosis Features
Grade 1 (mild) Pelvis 1 cm; physiological calcyceal dilatation
Grade 2 (moderate) Pelvis 1-1.5 cm; normal calyces
Grade 3 (severe) Pelvis >1.5 cm; slight calyceal dilatation
Grade 4 (severe) Pelvis >1.5 cm; moderate calyceal dilatation
Grade 5 (severe) Pelvis >1.5 cm; severe calyceal dilatation and atrophic cortex
Data from Fernback SK, Maizels M, Conway JJ. Ultrasound grading of hydronephrosis: Introduction to the system used by the Society of Fetal Urology. Pediatr Radiol 1993;23:478-480 and Grignon A, Filion R, Filiatrault D, et al. Urinary tract dilatation in utero: classification and clinical applications. Radiology 1986;160:645-647.

feature.caption: Differential Diagnosis of Etiology of Antenatal Hydronephrosis
feature.feature_body:
Diagnosis Features VCUG needed? Diuretic renography needed? Proportion of cases of hydronephrosis,
Transient hydronephrosis Resolves on its own; benign course. Majority of cases of ANH. No No 41-88%
Physiologic hydronephrosis Due to transient oliguria after birth; resolves after 48 hours. No No 15%
Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction Dilation of the renal pelvis without ureteral dilation. Intervention required in 19-25% of cases. Increased risk of concomitant VUR and MCDK. Optional Yes 10-30%
Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) Suggested by increased APPD after voiding on renal ultrasound. Retrograde flow of urine detected on VCUG. Yes If concerns for UPJ obstruction 10-20%
Megaureter Dilation of both the ureter and the renal pelvis on renal ultrasound. Suspected if ureter is dilated >7mm with renal parenchymal atrophy. No reflux noted on VCUG. Yes Yes 4-10%
Multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) Multiple cysts of varying sizes on ultrasound. Often associated with a duplicated collecting system or ectopic insertion of the ureter. Optional Optional, most cases already diagnosed prenatally 2%
Posterior urethral valves (PUV) Bilateral hydronephrosis on ultrasound with possible megacystitis or thick-walled bladder. Markedly dilated posterior urethra on VCUG. Yes No 1-2%
Prune-Belly syndrome Bilateral hydrouretereonephrosis with irregular abdominal circumference due to megacystitis and degeneration of abdominal wall musculature. Yes Optional Rare
Data from Sinha A, Bagga A, Krishna A, Bajpai M, Srinivas M, Uppal R, Agarwal I. Revised guidelines on management of antenatal hydronephrosis. Indian Pediatr 2013; 50: 215-231 and Nguyen HT, Herndon CD, Cooper C, Gatti J, Kirsch A, Kokorowski P, Lee R, Perez-Brayfield M, Metcalfe P, Yerkes E, Cendron M, Campbell JB. The Society for Fetal Urology consensus statement on the evaluation and management of antenatal hydronephrosis. J Pediatr Urol 2010; 6: 212–231.
